messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Navy Officer
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Miguel Alvarez is a 55-year-old Navy officer who came to treatment after years of trying to keep one part of his life sealed off from the rest. He grew up in the United States in a Latin American family and had spent much of his adult life in uniform, priding himself on steadiness, discipline, and the ability to act under pressure. The event that continues to return to him happened before his military career, when he was a young civilian living with relatives in a war zone. He describes a day of sudden violence in the neighborhood where he and other family members had believed they could remain out of the way and survive by staying careful. What stands out in the way Miguel tells it is not broad political context but a series of concrete moments: the crack of gunfire close enough to make everyone drop, the sharp smell of smoke and dust, the sight of terrified people trying to move at once, and his own awareness that others were looking to one another for cues about where to run and who needed help.

In those moments, Miguel remembers freezing and then moving in a way that has never felt like enough. He can recount trying to get down, trying to pull himself and others toward cover, but the part of the event that has remained most powerful for him is his conviction that he did not do more to stop what happened and did not protect the people he should have protected. He speaks about this with the certainty of a verdict rather than the uncertainty of a memory. In his mind, there was something a stronger man would have done, some decisive action that would have changed the outcome, and because he did not do it, he has come to believe he is weak. Even now, decades later, he says he will never forgive himself for failing others that day.

The memory does not come back to him in only one form. At times it arrives with such force that he feels as if he is back there completely. He does not merely think about the event; he re-enters it. He describes hearing the gunfire again, smelling the smoke, seeing the scene all at once with unnerving immediacy, as if the present moment has dropped away. During these episodes he may go quiet and rigid, his attention fixed somewhere beyond the room. At other times he can tell the story in a flat, detached way that unsettles him differently. Then he sounds almost like an observer reporting something that happened to someone else, with little feeling in his voice. He notices that numb version too and is disturbed by it, as if even his distance from the memory is another sign of failure.

These experiences have sat uneasily alongside his life as a Navy officer. His work environment is structured, demanding, and full of reminders of responsibility for others. In briefings, on base, and in everyday leadership situations, he is repeatedly put in positions where protection, judgment, and decisive action are central values. He does not report dramatic outward breakdowns at work, but the private meaning he gives the trauma is woven into how he experiences himself there. Moments when subordinates look to him for direction can stir the old thought with fresh force: a good man protects people; he failed to do that. The contrast between the competent officer others see and the younger civilian he still condemns inside has become increasingly painful. He carries himself with control, yet underneath he is often measuring himself against that moment and finding himself morally inadequate.

Over the years Miguel has spoken very little about the event, even with his partner. When memories break through vividly, he is left with intense guilt so immediate that it seems undeservedly current, as though the harm has just happened and he is again standing in the instant of not doing enough. When the memory comes back numb and distant, he does not feel relieved; instead he is troubled by the absence of feeling, interpreting that too through the lens of weakness and failure. The result has been a life in which the event is never fully absent. It appears in flashes, in self-judgments, and in quiet moments when he finds himself replaying what he should have done differently.

He sought help now because he has become tired of living under that internal accusation. As he gets older, he is less able to dismiss the idea that this is simply something he should carry alone. He is frightened that if he talks about the event in detail, the memory will become completely real again and overwhelm him with the same sensory force it has in the worst moments. He is equally frightened that nothing will change, that therapy might confirm what he already believes—that he was weak, that he failed to protect others, and that he does not deserve forgiveness. At the same time, what he hopes for is modest but deeply important to him: to speak about that day without being pulled entirely back into it, and to find some way of living with the memory that does not always end in judgment.
